title: Act V, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: At Philippi, Octavius notes the enemy has come down to fight. The generals meet and exchange insults: Antony mocks the conspirators' flattery of Caesar; Cassius reminds Brutus he should have killed Antony. Octavius refuses to give way to Antony's order on the field. Cassius tells Messala it is his birthday and that he now half believes in omens: eagles have left their banners and ravens fly overhead. Brutus and Cassius say farewell, uncertain whether they will meet again; Brutus says he would not go bound to Rome.

context.history: The battles of Philippi in Macedonia (42 BC) ended the republican cause. Cassius had followed Epicurus, whose followers did not believe omens.

significance: Octavius's quiet defiance of Antony foreshadows the future (he will become the emperor Augustus). Cassius's change of mind on omens and the farewells build dread.

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The parley shows the conspirators preparing for defeat even before the battle. Useful evidence: “This is my birth-day; as this very day / Was Cassius born” (Act V, Scene I, Cassius): Cassius notes it is his birthday: the day of birth may be the day of death. middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
